summary: Summation No. 32 reports on Occupation non-military activities in Japan for May 1948, with most economic statistics running through March or April. Politically the month was dominated by the Ashida coalition's dispute over suspending war-bond interest, settled by a one-year deferral, and by Cabinet struggles over the 1948-49 budget and local finance. The report reprints MacArthur's message and other statements on the first anniversary of the Constitution, the Cabinet's Second Economic White Paper and the Economic Stabilization Board's five-year rehabilitation plan. It records party conventions, the Diet's investigation of political donations, the dissolution of the purge committees with 301,815 persons purged, and war crimes trial totals. Economic sections give detailed output, trade, price, finance and labor series, including postwar highs in steel, paper and textiles. The social sections cover health, nutrition, repatriation, education, religion and the press. Historians will find the primary-source texts and monthly statistical series especially useful.
highlights: The Cabinet accepted Chief Cabinet Secretary Tomabechi's plan on 14 May, formally announced 22 May, deferring war-bond interest for one year from June, resolving a coalition split over the 460 million yen due.

MacArthur's 3 May message on the Constitution's first anniversary urged vigilance, local autonomy, free enterprise and a responsible press and labor, while Ashida and other leaders spoke before the Emperor at the Diet.

The Cabinet issued the Second Economic White Paper on 28 May, and the Economic Stabilization Board's 17 May draft five-year plan aims to restore the 1930-34 living standard by 1952, with coal at 44 million tons.
The purge committees were dissolved on 10 May under Cabinet Order No. 62, with 301,815 persons announced as purged; the Attorney-General's Investigation Bureau took over enforcement.
The Cabinet approved a 399.3 billion yen 1948-49 budget on 30 May after wrangling over rail and postal rates and wage base, while a 25.8 billion yen provisional budget passed 28 May.
April output set postwar records: pig iron 55,072 tons, steel ingots 118,557 tons, coke 233,940 tons, and paper, spun silk yarn, rayon and cotton and silk fabrics all reached postwar highs.
By 20 May, 666 war criminals had been tried and 617 convicted, including 95 sentenced to death; the Maritime Safety Board was activated 1 May and the first Impeachment Court president was elected.
Of 33,635 Japanese repatriated 30 April to 27 May, 97 percent came from Soviet areas, and the Ministry of Education's 7 May policy treated Korean schools separately.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover, contents for Parts I to IV with 109 numbered charts, and lists of charts, maps and graphs by subject, ending with Men of Japan.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of May 1948: no change in SCAP non-military organization, with paragraphs summarizing the political, economic and social developments detailed in Parts II to IV.

sections.title: Section 1: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: States that the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, underwent no change during May 1948.

sections.title: Section 2: Political Activities
sections.summary: Constitution anniversary on 3 May, war-bond interest dispute ending in a one-year deferral, 16 laws enacted, purge committees dissolved with 301,815 purged, Maritime Safety Board, and war crimes results (53 suspects, 44 convicted).

sections.title: Section 3: Economic Activities
sections.summary: April output rose in coke (233,940 tons), pig iron, steel, cement, paper and textiles. First-quarter trade deficit was $151.8 million; ration needs met from carryover stocks; labor calmer; tax receipts above estimate.

sections.title: Section 4: Social Activities
sections.summary: April saw 3,237 communicable disease cases, 123,511 orphans counted and 33,635 repatriates, 97 percent from Soviet areas. Also the 7 May Korean school policy, a new National Christian Council and 379 Meiji sites delisted.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Detailed political section: government and politics (Constitution anniversary, war-bond interest, White Paper, budget, parties, purge), public safety, and legal affairs and war crimes.

sections.title: Section 1: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Constitution anniversary, war-bond interest deferral, Second Economic White Paper, five-year rehabilitation plan, budget wrangling, Diet, party conventions, and the purge dissolution.

sections.title: Anniversary of Promulgation of the Constitution
sections.summary: 3 May anniversary: MacArthur's message urged vigilance, local autonomy, free enterprise and responsible press and labor. Ashida and other leaders spoke before the Emperor; fourteen first-year reforms were listed, from popular sovereignty to land reform.

sections.title: War Bond Interest Payment Issue
sections.summary: Coalition parties split over suspending war-bond interest (460 million yen due in June). Tomabechi proposed a one-year deferral 8 May; the Cabinet adopted it 14 May and announced it 22 May over financial-circle opposition.

sections.title: National Government
sections.summary: On 22 May the Cabinet set ten principles for administrative readjustment, shifting authority to local governments. Local bodies rallied 24 May; remaining demobilization work passed to civilian ministries 31 May, with about 500,000 servicemen still in Soviet areas.

sections.title: Second Economic "White Paper"
sections.summary: The Ashida cabinet's 28 May report finds living conditions hard but prospects brighter: coal reached 29.32 million tons (97.7 percent of target), rice quota met, note issue fell early 1948. It urges self-support.

sections.title: Foreword and Basic Conditions of Postwar Economy
sections.summary: Hard living conditions persist but coal output, expected Allied aid and full rice delivery brighten the outlook. Handicaps: war losses of about 20 percent of prewar assets (45.7 billion yen), low trade, rapid population growth.

sections.title: General Survey of Present Economic Conditions
sections.summary: Population reached 78.62 million through repatriation of 5.77 million. Industrial production averaged 43.1 percent of 1930-34 in fiscal 1947; rice crop 59.67 million koku; trade deficit 520 million dollars; transport remained the bottleneck.

sections.title: Coal Production Increase and Power Situation
sections.summary: Coal-mine priorities and the Emergency Coal Production Increase Program produced a record 2.95 million tons in December. Drought and typhoon damage caused power shortages; 30.5 billion kWh was generated in 1947.

sections.title: Situation in Manufacturing Industry
sections.summary: Output rose in all categories except food processing and crude oil, led by metals (71 percent) and chemicals (31 percent). Finished steel 569,727 tons; pig iron 411,462 tons; cement 1.28 million tons against a 1.67 million target.

sections.title: Production in Agriculture, Forestry and Aquatic Industries
sections.summary: Fertilizer for rice rose to 4.3 kan per tan, about 60 percent of demand. Rice (59.67 million koku) stayed below 1930-34 levels; the typhoon cost 2.5 million koku; fish output was 62 percent of prewar.

sections.title: Transportation and Communication
sections.summary: Government railways carried 112 million tons (85 percent of requirements); coastal shipping over 10.68 million tons, up 88 percent. Ports run at 40 to 60 percent of prewar capacity; Tokyo telephones fail in 54 of 100 calls.

sections.title: Foreign Trade Returns
sections.summary: In 1947 imports were 526 million dollars and exports 174 million, a 352 million deficit covered by United States relief funds. Textiles supplied over half of exports; 68.2 percent of imports went to prevent hunger and disease.

sections.title: Prospects for Foreign Trade
sections.summary: East Asia took 66.8 percent of exports while 88.3 percent of imports came from the United States. A 60 million dollar cotton loan helps, but dollar shortage and unsettled exchange rates remain obstacles.

sections.title: Trend of Inflation
sections.summary: Tokyo indexes of official, black-market and effective prices are tabulated. Black-market retail prices rose only 16 percent from November to February, against 68 percent a year earlier, after the price revision.

sections.title: Currency Situation
sections.summary: Bank of Japan note issue grew 103 billion yen in fiscal 1947, ending at 218.7 billion in March, with a 40 billion rise in December. January and February 1948 showed declines. Deposits fell short of the 232.3 billion yen needed.

sections.title: Balance of Government Finance
sections.summary: General Account near balance as a pay-tax campaign lifted collections to 124.9 billion yen by March. Income-tax payers rose to 28.6 percent of the population; Special Account borrowing reached 66.8 billion yen, mostly from the Bank of Japan.

sections.title: Recent Condition of Industrial Enterprise Finance and Savings Accounts
sections.summary: Industrial financing grew 167.5 billion yen, 32 percent through the Reconstruction Finance Bank; coal took 53 percent of its general-industry advances. The Bank of Japan absorbed 75 percent of RFB bonds; time deposits were 21 percent of savings.

sections.title: Recent Conditions of Enterprises
sections.summary: Enterprises face money shortage and deficits from power shortages and wages averaging 1.6 times July 1947 levels. Labor productivity was only 28 to 33 percent of 1935-37; the report urges efficiency and support for small firms.

sections.title: Wage and Living Cost
sections.summary: Average manufacturing wages rose from 964 yen (January 1947) to 3,224 yen (March 1948); government salaries reached 3,930 yen. Food took 67 percent of family spending; real wages stood near 30 percent of prewar.

sections.title: Demand and Supply of Living Necessities
sections.summary: Staple rations were fulfilled since August 1947 and the rice quota fully delivered by mid-March. Fresh food rations reached about 70 percent of purchases by February; clothing supply is at most two pounds per capita.

sections.title: Labor Situation
sections.summary: The 1 October 1947 census gave 33.88 million gainfully employed and 672,000 unemployed, probably underestimated. About 6.15 million essential workers received extra rations; unions numbered 36,471 with 5,993,613 members at end of November 1947.

sections.title: Construction Works
sections.summary: Flood restoration cost far exceeded the 5 billion yen appropriated for fiscal 1947; river control needs about 150 billion yen. 1.68 million chobu await afforestation, only 145 kilometers of road were repaired, and urban housing losses equal a third of floor area.

sections.title: "Japanese Economic Rehabilitation Plan"
sections.summary: The Economic Stabilization Board's first draft five-year plan, issued 17 May, aims to restore the 1930-34 living standard by 1952, with coal at 44,000,000 tons, exports of $1,646 million and 2,000,000 houses.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Calls 1948 a crossroads for real reconstruction toward a self-supporting economy. Stresses maximum production, curbing inflation, efficiency, a minimum living standard and mobilized domestic capital; outside aid depends on full use of Japan's own resources.

sections.title: Local Government
sections.summary: A national conference of town and village heads opened in Tokyo 13 May, with Ashida pledging resignation if popular support was lost. A 27 May compromise settled local finance at 199,700,000,000 yen.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Fourteen bills were introduced 25 April to 25 May and sixteen laws enacted, including Daylight Savings Time and Minor Offense. Oishi and Takahashi won the 21 May Miyagi by-election.

sections.title: Budget Action
sections.summary: A June provisional budget of 25,800,000,000 yen passed 28 May while the Cabinet disputed rail and postal rates, a 3,731 yen wage base and local finance. It approved a 399,300,000,000 yen 1948-49 budget 30 May.

sections.title: Civil Service Institute
sections.summary: On 14 May the Civil Service Institute graduated its first class of 354 from a 100-day course: 126 return to ministries, 226 join the National Personnel Commission. A second class runs 2 August to 1 October.

sections.title: Hoarded Goods and Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee
sections.summary: The Diet's Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee, after 16 sessions and 45 witnesses on the Tsuji case, urged curbs on secret political funds. Four perjury indictments followed 10 and 12 May; Deputy Prime Minister Nishio was touched by construction-firm donations.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Democrats held their convention 4-5 May and accepted the war-bond compromise. Social Democrats moved to unify; Democratic Liberals attacked the Cabinet, with three small groups joining 25 May; Ashida proposed barring Communists from office.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: Purge committees were dissolved 10 May under Cabinet Order No. 62. Of 717,415 persons screened since 1946, 129 were reinstated 22 May. The Attorney-General's Investigation Bureau, with eight regional offices, took over enforcement.

sections.title: Section 2: Public Safety
sections.summary: Hoarded goods recovered in April were worth 123,296,141 yen. March saw 180,850 offenses and 101,402 arrests; 36,000 new police were recruited; prisoners numbered 89,234. The Maritime Safety Board was activated 1 May.

sections.title: Section 3: Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The first Impeachment Court president was elected; the Administrative Execution by Proxy Law passed 6 May. By 20 May 666 war criminals had been tried, 617 convicted including 95 sentenced to death; Okada was sentenced to hang.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Detailed economic section covering thirteen subjects: agriculture, forestry, heavy industries, manufacturing, textiles, transport, communications, labor, trade, rationing, finance, property control and science.

sections.title: Section 1: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Tenant land sales were 104,014 cho in April (531,334 cumulative); 11,774 agricultural cooperatives approved. March milk output was 10,185,000 liters, marine production 111,575 tons; Bonin whaling landed 243 whales.

sections.title: Section 2: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: April log output fell to 63,490,300 cubic feet. April coal production was 2,572,400 tons, nine percent under quota; fiscal 1947 coal was revised to 29,335,500 tons; crude oil 15,630 kiloliters.

sections.title: Section 3: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: April coke reached 233,940 tons, a fifth consecutive postwar record; pig iron (55,072 tons) and steel ingots hit postwar highs. Cement was 169,050 tons; 10 tugs and 13 barges went to the USSR.

sections.title: Section 4: Manufacturing
sections.summary: March flour 103,664 tons, sake 747,060 hectoliters; April paper reached a postwar high. Electrical goods were hurt by labor trouble; alarm clock and phonograph record output set records.

sections.title: Section 5: Textile Industries
sections.summary: April set postwar highs in spun silk yarn, rayon and cotton and silk fabrics; raw silk was 10,310 bales, above the 10,000-bale goal. Raw cotton stocks fell 29,250,000 pounds.

sections.title: Section 6: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered commercial vehicles fell to 161,320, about 67 percent operable. Government railways carried 312,127,898 passengers and 9,787,700 metric tons of freight; power generation reached 3,878,000,000 kWh; gas curbs on industry extended to 1 August.

sections.title: Section 7: Communications
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved a bill 22 May creating a Ministry of Communications. April brought 1,303,346 telephones and 6,535,531 radio households; ministry employees numbered 438,836, with a March profit of 355,966,254 yen.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: Labor relations were calmer than at any time since mid-1947; May Day rallies drew 300,000 in Tokyo. The Diet unanimously backed rejoining the ILO. Unions numbered 30,199 with 6,390,227 members.

sections.title: Section 9: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: March imports were $40,160,265, about 77 percent from the United States; exports were $11,606,301, two thirds to Asia. Textiles were 69 percent of exports; first-quarter deficit with the United States was $133,121,288.

sections.title: Section 10: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Staple collections were negligible in May, the second month of rations from carryover stocks; 137,620 tons of imported food were authorized, including 97,620 tons of sugar. Incentive goods reached farmers and coal miners.

sections.title: Section 11: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes stood at 223.5 billion yen on 31 May. A 15 May financial reorganization budgeted about 18 billion yen for bank losses; RFB loans reached 64.3 billion yen; national debt was 358.3 billion yen.

sections.title: Section 12: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property worth 278,781 yen was taken into custody and 737,044 yen restituted. The SCAP custody account reached 368.4 million yen; 80 control organizations were ordered liquidated; 9,967 machine tools had been shipped to reparations claimants.

sections.title: Section 13: Science and Technology
sections.summary: Twenty-one observation groups studied the 9 May annular eclipse, mainly at Rebun Island. Japan Academy prizes went to Koga, Fujiwara, Kotani and Tomonaga; 2,353 standards were in effect and 346 patents granted in April.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Detailed social section: public health and welfare, and education, religion, cultural resources and media of expression.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: April recorded 3,237 communicable disease cases with no cholera; 123,511 orphans were counted. Unemployment insurance replaced allowances 1 May; population reached 79,690,953 and 33,635 persons were repatriated.

sections.title: Section 2: Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Ministry of Education announced a Korean schools policy 7 May and 107 million authorized textbooks. The National Christian Council was organized 17 May; 379 Meiji historic sites were declassified; three new SCAP libraries opened.
